transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-01-23
Start: 15:30 PST
Duration: 48 minutes (recorded)
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Dr. Priya Nair (CTO, Rivermark), Sam Reynolds (Head of IT), Lena Ortiz (CISO), Marco Li (DevOps), Kelsey Boyd (QA)

Summary:
Quick discovery for a potential on-prem, air-gapped Redwood Private deployment. Primary concerns: offline update process, hardware compatibility (older GPU fleet, change windows), KMS/HSM integration, auditability and rollback, and procurement timeline for a 3-month pilot.

Topics:
- Air-gapped update workflow (signed images, manual transfer)
- Hardware footprint (T4 nodes, limited H100 availability)
- Patch window & maintenance constraints (weekly/quarterly windows)
- Security: HSM, SSO, audit logs, data residency
- Pilot scope and success criteria

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. quick intro: I'm Maya, AE on Redwood, and Diego is our systems engineer. how's everyone?
[00:12] Dr. Priya Nair: Hi Maya, thanks. We've been evaluating options for models in a tightly regulated lab environment. main ask is we can't have nodes that phone home, and updates have to be done via tagged artifacts we approve.
[00:26] Diego Alvarez: Got it. That's pretty standard for air-gapped. we support signed release bundles and a manual import workflow. we do want to confirm the types of GPUs and whether secure boot or TPM is required.
[00:40] Sam Reynolds: For hardware, most of our fleet is older: a mix of RTX A5000 and a couple of rented A100s we get during heavier runs. H100s are not in our approved list. Also storage is NFS behind a firewall.
[00:57] Diego Alvarez: Ok A5000 and A100 — that's workable. we'll flag quantization and performance differences. one thing to note: certain kernel optimizations we use are tuned to newer drivers. we can provide a compatibility matrix, but there may be trade-offs.
[01:14] Lena Ortiz: Quick security note: we require HSM-backed keys for any persistent model encryption and an audit trail that ties requests to user identities. SSO is via SAML with our IdP. also, change control requires dual approval for any image pushed into production.
[01:32] Maya Chen: Understood. Redwood Private can be configured with KMS/HSM integrations and we support SAML SSO. for audit, our console ships audit logs and per-token tracing, but in air-gapped mode those logs can be stored locally and exported.
[01:45] Marco Li: How do you handle updates? Our security team will only accept updates delivered on a signed USB or via an internal package repo; no direct connections.
[01:58] Diego Alvarez: We have an offline updater flow: we build a signed artifact bundle (SHA and signature), you import it into your internal repo; an operator triggers the deployment via the local control plane. we also support a 'dry-run' validation on a staging node before rolling.
[02:16] Kelsey Boyd: Does the control plane sit on-prem too? If it's local, who manages failover?
[02:24] Maya Chen: For Private, the control plane can be run in your VPC/on-prem. options: a minimal control plane that you manage, or a hybrid where metadata is mirrored to our managed control plane — but in fully air-gapped scenarios you'd run the entire stack locally. failover is configured via your HA policy; Diego can detail clustering.
[02:40] Diego Alvarez: Right, we use a lightweight HA controller. in an air-gapped env, we ship a multi-node controller setup. the operator can bring nodes up manually and we have a token exchange process for initial bootstrap. note: bootstrap tokens are single use and are generated from the signed bundle.
[02:58] Dr. Priya Nair: I want to call out regulatory reviews: we need exportable attestation for what exact binaries are running and a reproducible build chain. can you provide SBOMs and build provenance?
[03:12] Diego Alvarez: Yes, we can provide SBOM, build hashes, and a manifest that maps which kernels and quantization profiles were used. small caveat: some third-party kernel blobs may be binary blobs with limited visibility, we'll flag which components are fully open.
[03:29] Sam Reynolds: On maintenance windows, our lab schedules zero-downtime windows are very rare. we prefer rolling restarts on a per-node basis and a manual canary window for any change.
[03:42] Maya Chen: Our rollout policies support canaries and automatic rollback on error. in air-gap, rollback requires re-importing a previous bundle unless you keep previous artifacts locally — which we'd recommend.
[03:55] Marco Li: About resource footprint — what's the minimum node count for a small pilot? we don't want to spin up too many GPUs quickly.
[04:03] Diego Alvarez: For a functional pilot (low qps, acceptance testing), you could start with 2 inference nodes + 1 controller node, ideally with at least 8-16GB of GPU memory each. if you only have A5000 with 24GB that's fine; throughput will differ versus A100.
[04:21] Kelsey Boyd: For QA we need deterministic outputs for a set of prompts. how do you version models and ensure no drift during quantization?
[04:30] Diego Alvarez: We support model pinning and deterministic seeds. quantization profiles are explicit and stored per model artifact; we also run evaluation harnesses tied to prompt sets so you can detect regressions.
[04:40] Dr. Priya Nair: On encryption — are model files encrypted at rest? and who holds the key?
[04:47] Maya Chen: Model files can be encrypted at rest with your KMS/HSM. Redwood Private can use your key material — nothing needs to leave your HSM. we can also support envelope encryption for added protection.
[04:58] Sam Reynolds: Network-wise, we have a one-way transfer process: approved media is scanned in an air-gapped staging network, then moved to production nodes. are there any special image signing or metadata requirements?
[05:10] Diego Alvarez: We'll provide signed bundles with a clear manifest and a signature you can verify using your internal tooling. we can sign with your key if you prefer — there's a model for customer-side signing during your CD process.
[05:25] Maya Chen: Do you have procurement time constraints? getting GPUs is taking 8-12 weeks for some SKUs.
[05:31] Dr. Priya Nair: Yes, procurement is a bottleneck. we likely won't have more A100s until Q2. the pilot must run on existing hardware.
[05:39] Diego Alvarez: Ok. we'll prioritize a compatibility report for A5000s. there will be throughput and latency numbers per model and quantization setting.
[05:49] Third-party mention / cross-talk (Speaker 1): someone asked about other vendors —
[05:54] Lena Ortiz: We also looked at Privatelabs; their onboarding looked lightweight but lacked the HSM integration. just flagging.
[06:02] Maya Chen: Good to know. we'll surface where Redwood differs — particularly on observability and rollback features.
[06:10] Marco Li: About logs — retention must be at least 3 years for audit. can you keep logs locally and export to our archival storage?
[06:19] Diego Alvarez: Yes, local retention configurable. we can write to your archival buckets and support WORM (write once read many) policies if your storage supports it.
[06:30] Kelsey Boyd: For the POC, what would success criteria look like? we need reliability, parity with hosted outputs, and an ops playbook.
[06:39] Maya Chen: Typical success criteria: 1) integration with your SAML IdP and HSM for key management, 2) deterministic model outputs for our eval prompt set within tolerance, 3) successful offline update using your import process, and 4) documented runbooks for operator tasks.
[06:56] Dr. Priya Nair: Timeline: we want a pilot started in Feb and complete a 3-month evaluation by end of April if procurement finishes.
[07:07] Maya Chen: That aligns. next steps: we'll send the security pack and hardware matrix; Diego will come for a half-day site survey and we'll draft a pilot SOW.
[07:18] Sam Reynolds: One more question on telemetry — do you need any outbound endpoints for crash reporting or do you rely solely on local logs?
[07:26] Diego Alvarez: For air-gapped you can choose to keep everything local. we can also support a push model where you export crash bundles manually to a support case. we won't require outbound telemetry.
[07:38] Kelsey Boyd: And what about software refresh cadence? quarterly?
[07:42] Maya Chen: Typical cadence is monthly security patches and feature releases every 6-8 weeks, but for air-gapped we can align to your change windows — we ship signed bundles on your schedule.
[07:55] Marco Li: Great. can you provide an estimated token/cost model for offline nodes? even a rough per-hour cost helps for procurement budgeting.
[08:03] Maya Chen: We'll include a cost worksheet in the SOW covering reserved vs burst models and a per-token proxy for inference cost, plus engineering hours for initial onboarding.
[08:15] Dr. Priya Nair: Ok thanks, that helps.
[08:18] Maya Chen: anything else before we close?
[08:22] Lena Ortiz: Please include our compliance checklist in the pack: HIPAA-adjacent controls, export controls, and SIEM integration notes.
[08:30] Maya Chen: will do. thanks everyone for the candid discussion, we'll follow up with the artifacts and try to get Diego onsite the week of Feb 2nd.
